title: A Bed for the Night
premise: Compare four of the town's lodging houses from the street and choose where a modest purse should ask first.

opening.text:
JAUNT: A BED FOR THE NIGHT. The sun is going down on the busiest summer Chicago has ever seen, and you have nowhere to sleep. The land office opened in May, and buyers and speculators 'filled the streets and overflowed improvised camps on the adjacent prairies'. The American counted some hundreds of strangers on top of the town's own two or three thousand people.

Four houses that take in strangers lie between the wagon yards of the west side and Lake Street. See what each one is like, decide whether cost or convenience comes first, and choose where to knock. Be warned: in this town, 'full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides'.

stops.text: The Western Hotel, Randolph and Canal. W. H. Stow built it with a forty-foot front, a sixty-foot wing and a wagon yard, the stopping place for farmers and teamsters coming in from the west; he dates it 1834, a chronology 1835. Back in 1831 the county fixed what an innkeeper could charge: 12½ cents for lodging for men, 25 for supper, 50 for keeping a horse all night. In a summer like this one, good luck finding a bed at those prices.

choices.label: Cost comes first
choices.consequence: You will ask after the plainer, cheaper bed.

choices.label: Convenience comes first
choices.consequence: You will ask after a bed close to the business of the town.

stops.narrative: Cost or convenience: settle it before you knock.

stops.text: Over the South Branch to Lake and Market and the Sauganash, repaired and newly fitted up in June. A week later the Democrat described 'the immense congregation of strangers crowding every room of our public houses', some 'sleeping on the floor'. The landlord, Mark Beaubien, had his own answer to a full house. He liked to say he 'kept hotel like —' somewhere not mentioned in polite company, and told how he would put a man to sleep on the floor, give him a blanket and, once the traveller was 'slumbering soundly', take it back for the next guest.
stops.narrative: A newly fitted house, and a landlord who counts his blankets.

stops.text: East to LaSalle, behind Peck's store: Mrs Rufus Brown's log house, one of the first-class boarding houses, Andreas says. A boarding house feeds you by the week at a common table, and it is packed: 'full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides.' On 13 June the American found strangers filling the public houses and the streets, and store houses thrown open for the emigrants who had no roof at all.
stops.narrative: A bed and a table by the week: the plainer choice.

stops.text: On along Lake to Dearborn: the Mansion House, Dexter Graves's log tavern of 1831, which got a frame front out to the street line two years later. Haddock, his son-in-law, kept it until 1835, then Abram Markle took it over; nobody wrote down the month, so either man may be behind the bar tonight. Almost opposite stands the first Tremont House. Time to choose.

choices.label: Ask first at Brown's
choices.consequence: A boarding-house place behind Peck's, if one is free.

choices.label: Ask first here on Lake Street
choices.consequence: A tavern bed at the Mansion House, if one is free.

choices.label: Ask first at the Sauganash
choices.consequence: A bed in the newly fitted house, if one is free.

stops.narrative: Choose where to ask first. Nobody promises a vacant room.

legs.note: East to the river and over the South Branch bridge between Lake and Randolph, then north to the Lake Street corner.
legs.story: Cross from the wagon trade to the river corner.

legs.note: East along Lake Street to LaSalle; Brown's stands behind Peck's corner store.
legs.story: From a hotel to a boarding house: a different kind of bed.

legs.note: On east along Lake Street to Dearborn.
legs.story: The last house, then your choice.

endings.text: Cost first, and you knock first at Mrs Brown's. If there is a corner of a bed, it is yours, and you may have company in it: in June 1835 every house in town was full.
Convenience first, and you ask first on Lake Street. If the house is full there is always the floor, and in June 1835 plenty of strangers slept on it.
You set out wanting one thing and chose by another, which a full town makes easy. Sleep with one hand on your blanket: Mark Beaubien is not the only landlord who counts them.

keepsake.title: A Place to Lay Your Head
keepsake.text: A fictional note of where you meant to ask for a bed in July 1835. It is not a receipt for a room.

evidence.text: W. H. Stow built the Western Hotel at the south-east corner of Randolph and Canal: a 40 ft front with a 60 ft wing, a large stable and a yard the wagon trains drove into, the stopping place for farmers and teamsters from the west.
evidence.locator: chicagology pre-fire page 278, Town of Chicago: W. H. Stow's account of the Western Hotel.

evidence.text: Stow dates his hotel to 1834; the hotel chronology says it opened in 1835.
evidence.reasoning: The structure record adopts the builder's own 1834 date over an undated chronology line, so the stop gives both dates and claims nothing about the house being open on a particular night.

evidence.text: The Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835 reported that the Sauganash had been repaired, fitted up and furnished with neatness and taste.
evidence.locator: 10 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 8), p. 2, col. 5, the paragraph on the town's public houses (claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001). Transcription-mediated reading.

evidence.text: The Sauganash stood at the south-east corner of Lake and Market Streets, on the east bank of the South Branch.
evidence.reasoning: The corner is given by the hotel chronology and the Chicago Landmark designation; the building's coordinate in the scene is the structure record's platted-corner derivation and carries the georeference's uncertainty of about 20 m.

evidence.text: The Chicago Democrat of 17 June 1835 wrote of 'the immense congregation of strangers crowding every room of our public houses, and every room in which they can obtain accommodations, even to the extent of sleeping on the floor'.
evidence.locator: 17 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 9), p. 2, col. 4, the editor's paragraph on the state of the streets (claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_17#c001). Transcription-mediated reading; the issue's interior editorial block prints 10 June.

evidence.text: The Chicago American of 13 June 1835 reported that strangers, some hundreds more than the town's estimated 2,500 to 3,000, filled its public houses and streets, and that store houses had been thrown open to the unsheltered emigrants.
evidence.locator: 13 June 1835 (Vol. I No. 2), p. 2, col. 1, the paragraph on the town's population (claim chicago_american_1835_06_13#c001). Transcription-mediated reading of a poor OCR line.

evidence.text: Andreas names Mrs Rufus Brown as keeper of one of the first-class boarding houses, and places Brown's log house as the first building in the rear of Peck's store.
evidence.locator: Vol. 1, printed p. 132, boarding-house paragraph; p. 303, Jeremiah Porter biography.

evidence.text: The boarding house is placed directly behind Peck's store at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle; its distance behind the store is not documented.
evidence.reasoning: Andreas gives the position only relative to Peck's store. The structure record sets the house directly south of the store's footprint on the same lot line and grades the coordinate reconstructed, so the stop calls the exact spot our placement.

evidence.text: The Mansion House was built in 1831 by Dexter Graves on Lake near Dearborn, set back from the street; two years later he built a frame addition in front that came out to the street line.
evidence.locator: Vol. 1, printed p. 635, the Mansion House paragraph of the hotels chapter.

evidence.text: 'The opening of a land office in May, 1835, added fuel to the already brilliant blaze of excitement'; crowds of buyers and speculators 'filled the streets and overflowed improvised camps on the adjacent prairies'. Sales of land 'to the amount of 370,043 acres were made in 1835'.
evidence.locator: p. 97-98, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 13137-13162 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: In 1831 the county authorities made a tariff of rates 'obligatory upon all inn-keepers': 25 cents for each breakfast and supper, 37½ for dinner, 25 for each horse feed, 50 for keeping a horse all night, 12½ for lodging for men, 25 for half a pint of wine, rum or brandy, 18¾ for gin, and 6¼ for a gill of whiskey.
evidence.locator: p. 560, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98764-98777 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Mark Beaubien used to say that he 'kept hotel like —' a place not commonly mentioned in refined circles, and explained it by telling how he put a man to sleep on the floor, 'gave him a blanket', and when the traveller was 'slumbering soundly' took the covering off him, 'bestowing it upon the next weary and drowsy guest who might happen to stand in need of it'.
evidence.locator: p. 560, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98740-98751 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The houses of 1834 were always full; and full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides.
evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1 on the houses of 1834, quoted on the card brown_mrs_rufus (data/residents/households/hh_brown_rufus.json).

evidence.text: Graves sold the house to Haddock, his son-in-law, who kept it until 1835, when it passed to Abram A. Markle; no source gives the month of the handover.
evidence.reasoning: Andreas, printed p. 635, gives the succession by year only. The structure record finds the Democrat naming the house Haddock's by June 1834 but nothing dating the passage to Markle inside 1835, so it declines to choose a keeper for 1 July 1835, and the stop does the same.

evidence.text: The Mansion House stood on the north side of Lake Street just east of Dearborn, almost opposite the first Tremont House.
evidence.reasoning: Andreas puts it on Lake near Dearborn, almost opposite the old Tremont House, and Caton recalls it just north of where the Tremont stood; the side of the street follows from those two statements, and the position along the block is the structure record's choice.

evidence.text: The visitor's search for a bed, the cost-or-convenience preference, the route order, the relative cost of the four houses, the choice of where to ask, the endings and the keepsake are invented connective narrative. No price, vacancy or booking is documented.
